title: Growth Mindset Standard
summary: Every therapist is expected to maintain a growth mindset — the willingness to learn, improve, receive correction, and develop professionally and personally.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, every therapist is expected to maintain a growth mindset — the willingness to learn, improve, receive correction, develop new skills, adapt to higher standards, and become better professionally and personally.
Being a good therapist is not about believing that you already know everything. It is about being open to learning, willing to improve, and committed to continuous development.
A growth mindset means understanding that skills can be developed through practice, discipline, feedback, repetition, consistency, correction, experience, and a willingness to learn from mistakes.
At Zura Spa, being teachable is part of being professional.
A therapist who is talented but unwilling to learn will eventually become limited. A therapist who remains teachable can continue to improve, regardless of their current level of experience.

sections.title: 1. Relevance of a Growth Mindset
paragraphs: A growth mindset is important because it:
list: Improves the quality of massage services.
Improves consistency between therapists.
Helps therapists develop new massage techniques and skills.
Makes practical assessments and corrections more effective.
Helps therapists identify weaknesses and work on them.
Prevents the same mistakes from being repeated continuously.
Builds confidence through competence.
Encourages therapists to take responsibility for their development.
Makes it easier to introduce new routines, standards, procedures, and services.
Encourages therapists to learn from one another.
Improves teamwork.
Creates an environment where knowledge can be shared freely.
Helps newer therapists develop faster.
Helps experienced therapists continue improving rather than becoming complacent.
Protects Zura Spa from declining service standards.
Allows the company to continually raise the quality of the client experience.
sections.closing: Growth is therefore not only beneficial to the individual therapist. The willingness of each therapist to grow directly affects the quality of the entire team.

sections.title: 2. The Therapist's Mindset Towards Growth
paragraphs: Therapists should have the mindset: "I may not know everything yet, but I can learn, practise, improve and become better."
A correction should not automatically be interpreted as an insult, a personal attack, disrespect, proof that the therapist is incapable, or an attempt to embarrass the therapist.
Correction should first be considered as information that may help improve performance.
The proper response should be: Listen → Understand → Practise → Correct → Improve.
Therapists should also understand that experience alone does not guarantee growth. A person may practise the same thing for many years while practising it incorrectly.
Years of experience are valuable only when experience is accompanied by learning and improvement.
list: Humility.
Discipline.
Practice.
Self-awareness.
Accountability.
Patience.
Consistency.
Willingness to leave one's comfort zone.
sections.closing: Growth requires all of the above.

sections.title: 3. What a Growth Mindset Looks Like
paragraphs: A therapist with a growth mindset:
list: Wants to understand why something is done.
Pays attention during training.
Takes assessment seriously.
Asks questions when something is unclear.
Accepts correction.
Attempts the corrected technique again.
Practises areas where they are weak.
Watches stronger therapists and learns from them.
Shares useful knowledge with colleagues.
Is willing to change an old habit when a better standard is introduced.
Does not feel threatened when another therapist performs better.
Learns from mistakes.
Takes responsibility when they get something wrong.
Looks for ways to improve the client's experience.
Takes pride in becoming better.
Seeks feedback rather than avoiding it.
Understands that mastery comes through repetition.
Recognizes that there is always another level of improvement.
sections.closing: A growth-minded therapist does not merely ask "Did I do it?" They ask "Did I do it properly, and how can I do it better?"

sections.title: 4. What the Opposite Looks Like — A Fixed or Resistant Mindset
paragraphs: The opposite of a growth mindset is a fixed, resistant or unteachable mindset.

This occurs when a therapist begins to believe: "I already know this." "Nobody needs to correct me." "This is how I have always done it." "I don't need to practise." "They are always finding fault with me." "If I don't know it already, then I am not good at it."
This mindset can appear in different ways.

sections.title: Defensiveness
paragraphs: Every correction immediately produces an excuse or argument. Instead of listening, the therapist concentrates on defending themselves.
list: "But that is not what I was taught."
"I have always done it this way."
"Other therapists do the same thing."
"The client did not complain."
"That is just how I massage."

sections.title: Refusal to Practise
paragraphs: The therapist understands that a skill needs improvement but repeatedly avoids practising it. They want to be considered competent without doing the work required to become competent.

sections.title: Repeated Mistakes Without Improvement
paragraphs: Making a mistake is not automatically a problem. Continuing to make the same mistake while refusing correction is the problem.

sections.title: Pride
paragraphs: The therapist believes that admitting they do not know something makes them look weak. This can cause them to pretend they understand, avoid asking questions, reject help, perform techniques incorrectly, and become uncomfortable when someone else knows more.

sections.title: Resistance to New Standards
paragraphs: Whenever Zura Spa changes or improves a procedure, the therapist responds: "The old way was fine." Instead of learning the new standard, they continue doing what is convenient for them.

sections.title: Comparing Instead of Learning
paragraphs: Instead of observing a stronger therapist and learning from them, the therapist becomes jealous, competitive, discouraging, critical or defensive.
The question changes from "What can I learn from this person?" to "Why are they being praised?"

sections.title: Taking Correction Personally
paragraphs: The therapist interprets correction of a technique as rejection of themselves as a person. This prevents productive feedback.

sections.title: Blaming Others
paragraphs: When something goes wrong, the client is blamed, the co-therapist is blamed, reception is blamed, management is blamed, or training is blamed.
The therapist rarely asks: "What could I have done better?"

sections.title: Performing Only When Being Watched
paragraphs: The therapist follows standards during assessment or when supervisors are present but returns to careless habits afterwards. That is not growth. That is temporary compliance.

sections.title: 5. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate a Resistant Mindset
paragraphs: Zura Spa can tolerate a therapist who does not yet know something. Zura Spa can train someone who needs improvement. Zura Spa can correct a mistake. Zura Spa can develop a therapist who is inexperienced.
What cannot become acceptable is: refusing to learn, refusing to practise, refusing correction, repeatedly resisting standards, and allowing pride to prevent improvement.
A skill gap can be trained. An unwillingness to learn prevents training from working.
A therapist who says, "I don't know, but teach me," can develop. A therapist who says, "I already know and nobody can tell me anything," becomes increasingly difficult to develop.
This is why persistent resistance to growth cannot be treated as a harmless personality difference. It affects the business, the clients and the entire team.

sections.title: 6. Impact of a Poor Growth Mindset on the Team
paragraphs: A resistant mindset rarely affects only one therapist. It gradually affects everyone around that therapist.

sections.title: It Slows Down Training
paragraphs: When one person repeatedly resists correction, supervisors and experienced therapists spend unnecessary time correcting the same issue. That time could have been used to develop the entire team.

sections.title: It Creates Frustration
paragraphs: It becomes frustrating for colleagues when they repeatedly support, correct or assist someone who refuses to make an effort to improve. Eventually, good team members may stop wanting to help.

sections.title: It Weakens Team Standards
paragraphs: If one therapist is allowed to repeatedly ignore standards without correction, other therapists may begin to think: "If they can do it, why should I follow the standard?" One person's resistance can therefore gradually reduce discipline across the team.

sections.title: It Creates Inconsistency for Clients
paragraphs: One therapist follows the Zura routine properly. Another therapist refuses to change. Another therapist performs a different method. The result is that clients receive completely different experiences depending on who attends to them. This damages the meaning of a Zura Spa standard.

sections.title: It Makes Teamwork Difficult
paragraphs: Massage, especially 4-hands massage, requires therapists to listen, adjust, synchronize, support one another, and accept direction. A therapist who refuses feedback can become difficult to work with. This can affect the client's relaxation and the co-therapist's performance.

sections.title: It Discourages Strong Performers
paragraphs: Therapists who train seriously, practise, follow standards, accept correction, and improve consistently can become discouraged if someone who refuses to improve is allowed to behave as though the standards do not matter. This creates a sense of unfairness.

sections.title: It Produces Blame Instead of Solutions
paragraphs: A growth-oriented team asks: "What happened and how do we improve it?" A resistant team asks: "Whose fault is it?" Once blame becomes more important than learning, improvement becomes difficult.

sections.title: It Reduces Psychological Safety for Learning
paragraphs: Team members should feel comfortable saying: "I don't know." "Please show me." "Can we practise this again?" If people are mocked, defensive or overly competitive, therapists begin hiding their weaknesses instead of improving them.

sections.title: It Can Spread Negativity
paragraphs: Statements such as "This training is unnecessary," "They are doing too much," "I don't need this," "Don't mind them," and "Just do your own thing" can gradually influence other therapists. A negative mindset can spread faster than a positive one if it is allowed to become normal.

sections.title: 7. Impact on the Client
paragraphs: A therapist's unwillingness to grow can eventually reach the client. It can lead to:
list: Poor pressure control.
Weak massage technique.
Poor client communication.
Failure to identify pain points.
Poor synchronization during 4-hands massage.
Inconsistent routines.
Poor hygiene habits.
Poor room conduct.
Repeated client complaints.
Failure to follow improved service standards.
sections.closing: The client should never have to suffer because a therapist refuses to learn. This is one of the strongest reasons growth mindset is a standard rather than a suggestion.

sections.title: 8. What Therapists Should Do
list: Be open to learning.
Accept constructive feedback professionally.
Ask questions when something is unclear.
Admit when they do not know something.
Practise skills that require improvement.
Repeat techniques after correction.
Attend assessments and training seriously.
Observe experienced therapists and learn from their strengths.
Share useful knowledge.
Help colleagues improve.
Receive help without feeling embarrassed.
Adapt when Zura Spa introduces a new standard.
Take responsibility for mistakes.
Set personal improvement goals.
Apply lessons from previous corrections.
Demonstrate improvement over time.
Continue learning even after becoming experienced.
Encourage colleagues who are trying to improve.

sections.title: 9. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Believe that they already know everything.
Reject correction automatically.
Argue every time feedback is given.
Become hostile because of assessment results.
Ignore a correction after acknowledging it.
Deliberately continue doing something against the standard.
Repeatedly make excuses for the same weakness.
Refuse to practise.
Pretend to understand rather than ask questions.
Hide mistakes.
Blame others instead of taking responsibility.
Use seniority as an excuse for refusing correction.
Say, "This is how I have always done it," as a reason to reject a better method.
Discourage therapists who are learning.
Mock someone because they are practising.
Become jealous of another therapist's improvement.
Withhold useful knowledge to maintain an advantage over colleagues.
Treat another therapist's success as a personal threat.
Follow standards only when supervisors are present.
Encourage others to ignore company procedures.
Spread negativity about training and assessments.
Treat repeated correction as harassment simply because the therapist does not want to change.
Allow ego to become more important than client satisfaction.
Expect promotion, recognition or greater responsibility without demonstrating growth.

sections.title: 10. Correction Is Not the Same as Condemnation
paragraphs: Zura Spa must also maintain a healthy approach to correction.

Growth mindset does not mean therapists cannot ask questions, management is automatically correct about everything, feedback should be disrespectful, a therapist cannot explain what happened, someone should be embarrassed publicly, or mistakes should be used to insult people.
Correction should be clear, respectful, specific, relevant, practical, and focused on improvement.

A therapist should therefore be able to respectfully ask: "Please, can you show me how you want this done?" or "Can you explain what I should improve?" That is not resistance. That is part of learning.

sections.title: 11. How We Respond to Mistakes
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: A mistake + willingness to learn = training opportunity. Weakness + consistent practice = development. Correction + improvement = growth.
But: Repeated mistake + refusal to learn = performance concern. Repeated correction + deliberate resistance = disciplinary concern.
The emphasis is not on punishing someone for being imperfect. The emphasis is on ensuring that everyone remains willing to improve.

sections.title: 12. Growth Must Be Visible
paragraphs: Growth mindset should not exist only in words. If a therapist repeatedly says "I understand" but nothing changes, then learning has not yet taken place.

Improvement should gradually become visible in massage technique, pressure control, client handling, communication, hygiene, room conduct, synchronization, routine compliance, professionalism, teamwork, and reliability.
The evidence that feedback has been received is usually changed behaviour.

sections.title: 13. The Team Responsibility
paragraphs: Growth is an individual responsibility, but Zura Spa should also be a learning team.

Therapists should teach what they know, correct respectfully, practise together, encourage improvement, share useful techniques, celebrate progress, support weaker team members, avoid humiliating others, and create an environment where asking questions is normal.
The objective is not to prove "I am better than you." The objective is: "Let us become better together."
When one therapist improves, the team becomes stronger. When the team becomes stronger, the client receives a better experience.

sections.title: 14. Zura Spa Growth Standard
paragraphs: LEARN → ACCEPT → PRACTISE → APPLY → IMPROVE → REPEAT

Every therapist should regularly ask: What do I need to learn? What correction have I received? Have I actually applied it? What weakness do I need to practise? What am I doing better today than before? What can I learn from the people around me?
At Zura Spa, perfection is not the expectation. Progress is.
We do not expect every therapist to know everything. We do expect every therapist to remain teachable.
Not knowing is acceptable. Refusing to learn is not.
Making a mistake is acceptable. Refusing to correct it is not.
Having a weakness is acceptable. Choosing not to work on it is not.
Because at Zura Spa, an unwillingness to grow does not affect only one person. It affects the therapist, the co-therapist, the team, the client, and ultimately the Zura Spa standard.

remember: Being teachable is part of being professional. Progress is the expectation — not perfection.
